ethiopia.title: As Conflict Spreads From Moyale to Borana, Cross Border, Domestic Livestock Markets Grind to a Halt
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: As Conflict Spreads From Moyale to Borana, Cross Border, Domestic Livestock Markets Grind to a Halt - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: As Conflict Spreads From Moyale to Borana, Cross Border, Domestic Livestock Markets Grind to a Halt 11 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — A conflict that erupted in Moyale and spread to different parts of Borana, in southern Oromia, has entered its third week, severely disrupting daily life and bringing the areas main livestock market, a critical pillar of its economy, to a near standstill, residents told Addis Standard. The ongoing fighting has disrupted livestock trade, driven down prices and left pastoralist communities grappling with mounting economic hardship as traders from across Ethiopia and neighboring Kenya withdraw from the region's major markets. Bulee Waaqoo, a resident of Yabello District in the South Oromia Zone, told Addis Standard that vibrant livestock trading across Borana has virtually ground to a halt since the fighting began. He said that nearly three weeks of insecurity have significantly eroded the value of pastoralists' livestock assets. A young bull that previously sold for between 120,000 and 150,000 Birr now fetches only 70,000 to 90,000 Birr, he said. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "Traders coming from neighboring Kenya who used to purchase livestock from famous markets such as Dubuluq and Haroo Bakkee have completely stopped coming. Consequently, the cross-border livestock trade into Kenya has been entirely severed. Furthermore, buyers from various parts of Ethiopia have also stayed away since the fighting started, leaving the region's market completely paralyzed," he said. Another resident, Culluu Jaatanii, from Dubuluq town, told Addis Standard that livestock trading across Borana Zone has declined sharply, exposing pastoralist households to severe economic hardship. He said that following Haroo Bakkee, Dubuluq hosts one of the largest livestock markets in the zone, attracting numerous buyers, including traders from Kenya's Marsabit county, Moyale, Sololo and other areas. "Now, all these traders are gone. The only people buying livestock are local butchers, who buy from us at very low prices. If the price suits you, you sell; if not, you leave it. But if you don't sell, your problems don't go away, so our only option is to sell our livestock at dirt-cheap prices," he told Addis Standard , describing the difficulties residents have faced over the past three weeks. He added, "Where we previously sold one head of cattle to cover an expense, we are now forced to sell two because prices have dropped so low. This has severely hurt our economy." A resident of Haroo Bakkee town also told Addis Standard that the town's Sunday livestock market, which typically attracts thousands of animals and traders from different parts of the country, has experienced a dramatic decline in activity. "At the very least, traders from many places would arrive on Sundays to buy livestock, loading roughly 40 large trucks to transport cattle to cities like Adama, Mojo, and Finfinnee," he said. "Now, at most, only three or fewer trucks arrive. This highlights how few cattle are being purchased and how traders from the central parts of the country are absent." He further recalled that large bulls and camels were previously purchased and transported across the border into Kenya. "Now, all of that has stopped," he said. A resident of Nageellee Borana town similarly reported a sharp decline in livestock prices since the conflict began. He said a bull that previously sold for 170,000 Birr now fetches approximately 130,000 Birr. He explained that the town's livestock market previously attracted large numbers of buyers who purchased cattle for transportation across the Kenyan border. Traders from different backgrounds, including Somalis, also regularly visited the market. "Now all these traders are gone, with only a few coming exclusively via the Adama route. Even then, instead of buying at our asking prices or what we used to sell for, they purchase from us strictly on their own terms," he said. An economist at Borana University, who spoke to Addis Standard , said the decline in the number of heavy transport trucks arriving at Haroo Bakkee market--from approximately 40 to three or fewer--indicates that the estimated market activity has contracted by more than 90%. "The Borana livestock market is not just an income source for pastoralists; it also sustains small traders, livestock loaders and unloaders, vehicle owners, and local eateries. The absence of these trucks has left thousands without work, creating a complex economic crisis in the region," the economist said. He further noted that the withdrawal of traders from Kenya, particularly Marsabit, Moyale and Sololo, as well as buyers from central Ethiopia, has effectively eliminated market competition. "Previously, because domestic and foreign traders competed against each other, pastoralists received better prices. Now, with so few buyers, the market has fallen into the hands of a select few. Beyond cutting off border foreign exchange earnings, this also severely reduces the revenue the zonal administration collects from market taxes," he explained. The economist also warned that the sharp decline in livestock prices has forced pastoralists who previously sold a single animal to meet household expenses to sell two or more, further depleting their assets. "These dynamics risk causing severe long-term damage," he cautioned. "Pastoralists who used to sell one bull to buy multiple quintals of grain can now only afford a few quintals. This exposes the region's population to the threat of hunger and malnutrition." He also highlighted the long-term consequences of pastoralists selling their livestock at distressed prices to meet immediate needs. "In particular, when breeding cows and young bulls, which form the future economic foundation of households, are sold off, pastoralists will have no means to recover once the war ends. This will lead to deep-rooted poverty, requiring many years for the region to bounce back," he said. The economist called for three urgent interventions to prevent further economic losses among pastoralist communities: government and humanitarian organizations should use cooperatives to facilitate the purchase of livestock at fair prices and transport them to central markets; emergency food assistance should be provided to prevent households from selling livestock at reduced prices to purchase grain; and major trade routes should be secured to enable traders to resume business safely. The residents and the economist interviewed by Addis Standard warn that continued disruption could leave thousands of pastoralist households facing hunger, asset depletion and prolonged poverty, with the region's economic recovery potentially taking years. Residents report that the fighting has led to a near-total halt in livestock trade, with prices plummeting as traders from Ethiopia and neighboring Kenya withdraw from the region. For instance, the price of a young bull has dropped from 120,000-150,000 Birr to just 70,000-90,000 Birr. The absence of traders has left local pastoralists vulnerable, forcing them to sell livestock at significantly reduced prices to meet immediate needs. An economist noted that market activity has contracted by over 90%, affecting not only pastoralists but also small traders and local businesses. The situation poses a risk of long-term economic damage, with potential hunger and malnutrition threatening the community. Urgent interventions are needed to stabilize the market and support affected households.

ethiopia.title: U.S. Senators Send Second Letter to Rubio Urging Action to Avert Widening Conflict in Ethiopia
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: U.S. Senators Send Second Letter to Rubio Urging Action to Avert Widening Conflict in Ethiopia - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: U.S. Senators Send Second Letter to Rubio Urging Action to Avert Widening Conflict in Ethiopia 11 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — A group of U.S. Democratic senators has sent a second letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio urging intensified American diplomatic intervention to prevent renewed fighting in Ethiopia and escalating tensions with Eritrea from developing into a wider regional conflict. The November 10 letter, led by Senator Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, warns that renewed hostilities in Tigray, continuing conflicts in Amhara and Oromia, and deteriorating relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea risk triggering a multi-front war with consequences extending across the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea. "We write to urge sustained and coordinated diplomatic engagement to address fighting between armed groups and the Ethiopian military and escalating tensions with Eritrea," the senators wrote. They warned that renewed hostilities have "shattered the fragile peace in Tigray established by the 2022 Pretoria Agreement," which ended the two-year war between federal forces and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). The conflict left an estimated 600,000 people dead and approximately 120,000 victims of conflict-related sexual violence, according to figures cited in the letter. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The senators cited a series of developments they said had heightened the risk of regional escalation, including renewed clashes in Tigray since August, Ethiopian government drone strikes, and continuing fighting between federal forces and Fano fighters in Amhara, alongside the insurgency in parts of Oromia. They specifically pointed to a September 20 drone strike that hit a Catholic Relief Services aid convoy carrying U.S.-funded assistance. The letter also raised concerns over reports of Eritrean forces operating inside Tigray, severed diplomatic ties between Addis Abeba and Asmara, reciprocal diplomatic expulsions involving Egypt, and the potential spillover of the war in neighboring Sudan. The lawmakers outlined seven measures they want Washington to pursue. They called on the State Department to help U.S. citizens in Ethiopia access emergency assistance and evacuation support if security conditions deteriorate, while intensifying diplomatic efforts to secure an immediate ceasefire and renewed mediation involving all relevant parties. They also urged Washington to make clear that any Ethiopian attempt to forcibly access Eritrea's Port of Assab "will not be supported or accepted by the United States." On civilian protection, the senators called for pressure on all parties to end the use of drones and heavy weapons in civilian areas, protect farmland and harvests, maintain communications access, and safeguard civilian infrastructure. They further urged the administration to suspend new arms sales to Ethiopia while hostilities continue, use its diplomatic leverage with Eritrea, Egypt, Sudan and other regional actors to discourage military intervention or support for armed groups, and increase humanitarian assistance amid drought, disrupted harvests and displacement. The lawmakers also called for the reinstatement of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for eligible Ethiopian nationals in the United States, citing renewed concerns over the safety of returns. "The situation could lead to a multi-front conflict that would risk destabilizing Ethiopia, the broader Horn of Africa, the Red Sea, our partners in the Gulf, and vital shipping lanes," the senators warned, urging Washington to deploy additional diplomatic and policy measures before the situation deteriorates further. In mid-October, Rubio called on countries in the Horn of Africa t o respect their neighbors' sovereignty and territorial integrity, urging restraint, de-escalation and dialogue amid heightened tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea. During a telephone conversation with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali, Rubio stressed that "all countries in the Horn of Africa must respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors and avoid cross-border incursions." He cautioned that "the region cannot tolerate more conflict," according to the U.S. Department of State's official readout of the call The latest appeal follows an earlier warning in September. On September 28, six U.S. senators, also led by Shaheen, called on Rubio to intervene following renewed fighting in Tigray and neighboring Afar and Amhara regions. They warned that the African Union-brokered Pretoria Agreement was unraveling and urged Washington to engage the Ethiopian federal government, TPLF leadership and associated armed groups to halt hostilities and return to mediation. That earlier intervention also criticized the Trump administration's decision to allow sanctions targeting individuals and entities accused of human rights abuses during the Tigray war to expire under Executive Order 14046. The senators cited a drone strike on a vehicle transporting U.S.-funded food assistance for internally displaced people in northwestern Tigray, warning that the attack had disrupted humanitarian deliveries. The renewed congressional pressure comes as Washington's political landscape shifts following the November 3 midterm elections. Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress, flipping at least seven Senate seats and gaining a substantial majority in the House, according to Associated Press projections. The results will give Democrats control of the Senate and House when the new Congress convenes in January 2027, potentially strengthening the influence of lawmakers pressing for a more assertive U.S. approach to Ethiopia and the wider region. ethiopia.summary: A group of U.S. Democratic senators has sent a second letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, urging immediate diplomatic action to prevent escalating conflict in Ethiopia. The letter, led by Senator Jeanne Shaheen, highlights the risks of renewed fighting in Tigray and ongoing tensions with Eritrea, which could lead to a broader regional conflict. The senators express concern over the fragile peace established by the 2022 Pretoria Agreement, warning that recent hostilities have already resulted in significant casualties and humanitarian crises. They propose several measures, including facilitating U.S. citizen evacuations, securing a ceasefire, and suspending arms sales to Ethiopia. The senators also emphasize the need for civilian protection and increased humanitarian assistance amid ongoing violence and displacement. This renewed appeal follows a previous letter in September, reflecting growing congressional pressure for a more assertive U.S. response to the situation in Ethiopia and the Horn of Africa.

ethiopia.title: A Country Divided, a Region On Edge - Somalia Caught in the Crossfire of Foreign Rivalries
ethiopia.content: Somalia: A Country Divided, a Region On Edge - Somalia Caught in the Crossfire of Foreign Rivalries - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Somalia: A Country Divided, a Region On Edge - Somalia Caught in the Crossfire of Foreign Rivalries 11 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Somalia is approaching a dangerous political and security crossroads. A confrontation over constitutional amendments, presidential tenure, and elections is increasingly intersecting with competition among foreign powers for influence across the Horn of Africa, the Gulf of Aden, and the Red Sea. The danger is not simply that external governments back opposing Somali actors. It is that foreign rivalries can supply the resources, diplomatic protection, and military assistance that allow an unresolved domestic crisis to harden into a prolonged, multi-sided conflict. In an analysis published on 16 October 2026 , Chatham House argues that Somalia's instability is being compounded by sharpened regional rivalries. It identifies Turkey and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as particularly consequential actors within wider alignments involving Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Eritrea, Israel, and Ethiopia. The timing matters. In the final days of October 2026, the United Nations political mission is closing after a ceremony in Mogadishu on 26 October, the electoral commission has fixed a contested 2027 election calendar, and the president has invited opposition groups to a national forum from 14 to 18 November that major opposition coalitions have not yet agreed to attend. The issue is therefore larger than a quarrel between Mogadishu and its opponents: Somalia's divisions are entangled with the calculations of states seeking ports, maritime routes, military partnerships, and influence. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines A distinction is essential. Foreign competition does not automatically produce war, and external governments are not the sole authors of Somalia's instability; Somali elites retain agency and responsibility. The more immediate danger lies in the interaction between political exclusion, weak dispute-resolution mechanisms, fragmented security institutions, and foreign relationships that can shift the balance among factions. The question is whether Somalia's leaders and partners can stop these overlapping interests from turning a constitutional dispute into a conflict that is hard to contain. Constitutional Dispute: Domestic fault line beneath foreign competition On 8 March 2026, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud signed into law a constitutional package replacing the 2012 provisional charter. It extended presidential and parliamentary terms from four years to five and moved the country toward direct elections. Under the earlier terms, parliament's mandate was due to end on 14 April and the president's on 15 May 2026. When the original presidential term lapsed in May, the government declared a transition period . The federal government maintains that the changes allow it to remain in office until May 2027. Opposition leaders argue that the process lacked consensus and cannot settle the question of mandates. The Somali Future Council (SFC), which includes the leaders of Puntland and Jubaland, warned that the country risked operating under two competing constitutional frameworks. The dispute turned violent in early June, when fighting broke out in Mogadishu between government forces and opposition-aligned militias. Political talks held from 13 to 15 May ended without resolving the key electoral disputes , according to the UN mission, and a Turkish-brokered process in July stalled when the Puntland and Jubaland delegations withdrew. The president has since declared that his presidency continues until May 2027 , while opposition leaders say his mandate has expired. October has sharpened rather than resolved the impasse. On 15 October, the National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission announced elections to both houses of parliament on 15 April 2027 and a presidential vote on 15 May 2027, the latter based on a five-year term running from the president's swearing-in. According to the commission's timetable , registration reopens from 1 to 22 November, parliamentary candidate lists are due on 22 November, and campaigning begins on 27 February 2027, all under one-person-one-vote. Opposition parties boycotted the parliamentary vote that approved the constitutional changes and, with Puntland and Jubaland, have rejected the timetable. The SFC called for an immediate resumption of negotiations . Former president Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, who has petitioned the Supreme Court to annul the amendments, warned that a contested process could produce parallel elections and even civil conflict. Doubts about the electoral machinery are not confined to the opposition: in August the Supreme Court annulled the results of Galmudug's parliamentary and local council elections. Foreign rivalries do not create every domestic grievance, but their support can make confrontation harder to contain." Against this backdrop, the presidency formally invited opposition groups on 26 October to national talks in Mogadishu from 14 to 18 November, a day after the president said his government was ready to sit down with anyone who holds a different view . The Somali Non-State Actors network, the largest civil society grouping, welcomed the invitation . At the time of writing, the main opposition coalitions had not publicly confirmed attendance, and the opposition has not presented a common front. Its main bloc had earlier asked the UN Secretary-General to convene talks on equal terms, a request that now arrives as the UN's political mission closes. The crisis also strains the federation itself. Puntland and Jubaland are the most prominent opponents of Mogadishu's approach, and relations with South West State deteriorated, culminating in federal military action and a change of administration in Baidoa in March 2026, according to the European Union Agency for Asylum's June 2026 security assessment . When rival parties no longer trust constitutional procedures or mediation to protect their interests, the incentive to seek security through armed allies grows; when those parties also have relationships with competing external powers, a domestic dispute becomes internationalized. Foreign governments did not create every grievance, but their support can influence whether Somali actors compromise or conclude that confrontation is sustainable. Turkey and the UAE: Strategic rivalry at the center of the crisis Turkey has built an extensive partnership with the federal government, combining humanitarian aid, infrastructure, diplomacy, and military training. Its TURKSOM facility has trained Somali personnel in Mogadishu since 2017, and Turkish companies have interests in the capital's port and airport. A ten-year defense and economic framework signed in February 2024 commits Turkey, according to the Somali government's published summary , to help build, train, and equip the Somali navy and to expand cooperation on maritime security and marine resources. For Ankara, Somalia offers influence and a position near vital sea lanes; for Mogadishu, military capacity, investment, and a powerful partner. Yet concentrating engagement on the federal government creates a political complication. When Mogadishu and the member states fall out, regional leaders may read federal-Turkish cooperation as strengthening one side of an unresolved contest. The limits of Turkish mediation illustrate the point: when Turkish intelligence officials convened preliminary talks, Puntland and Jubaland boycotted them , insisting that Ankara is not neutral. The EastAfrican noted in June that the Turkish embassy was the one key mission that had not joined other embassies' calls for dialogue after the Mogadishu clashes, which angered the opposition. Chatham House has reported allegations that Turkish fighter jets were involved in fighting near Baidoa. The claim is serious but unconfirmed by Ankara and should not be treated as established fact; if verified, direct participation against armed political opponents would mark a significant escalation. The UAE represents a different model, combining commercial investment, port operations, security cooperation, and direct engagement with regional administrations. DP World holds a major concession at Berbera in Somaliland, Emirati interests extend to Bosaso in Puntland, and the UAE has also maintained ties with Jubaland. On 12 January 2026, the federal government announced the cancellation of its agreements with the UAE, including those on ports, defense, and security, citing sovereignty and territorial integrity. Somaliland, Puntland, and Jubaland rejected the move, and Reuters reported that the dispute exposed Mogadishu's limited ability to enforce its decisions across a fragmented federal system. The underlying issue is not whether Somalia should cooperate with Turkey or the UAE; a sovereign state may keep several partners. The problem arises when external partnerships become entangled with competing claims to domestic authority, and agreements with different Somali administrations become instruments in a wider struggle for influence. The Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden: Why Somalia matters to foreign powers Somalia's coastline faces the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, near routes linking the Red Sea, the Suez Canal, and global markets, and close to the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Instability around the Red Sea and Yemen has raised the strategic value of its ports and waters. Properly governed, these assets could generate revenue, trade, and maritime security. But geography also attracts competition for port concessions, naval access, and intelligence relationships, and commercial investments acquire strategic meaning when regional conflicts intensify. This creates a structural risk. The more divided Somalia becomes, the more valuable competing local partners appear to outsiders, and the more outsiders invest in rival relationships, the harder it is for Somali leaders to reach a common settlement. Somalia risks becoming a place where other states' objectives are pursued through competing domestic alliances rather than through a coherent national framework. Ethiopia, Somaliland, and Israel: Sovereignty dispute widens Relations among Somalia, Ethiopia, and Somaliland involve the basic questions of territorial integrity and sea access. In January 2024, Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with Somaliland on access to the sea, which Somalia rejected as an agreement over its territory concluded without its consent. Turkey then facilitated the Ankara Declaration of 11 December 2024 , in which both countries reaffirmed sovereignty and territorial integrity while recognizing the benefits of Ethiopian sea access through arrangements under Somalia's sovereign authority. It showed that external involvement is not inherently destabilizing: a foreign power can facilitate negotiation rather than strengthen one side. The sovereignty question acquired a new dimension in December 2025, when Israel became the first country to formally recognize Somaliland, as Reuters reported on 26 December 2025 . Somalia condemned the move, and Turkey, Egypt, Djibouti, and the African Union rejected the recognition. For Somaliland, recognition has long been a central objective; for Mogadishu, it challenges the integrity of the state; for outside powers, ties with Somaliland carry implications for maritime access and Red Sea influence. The greatest danger is the convergence of domestic exclusion, fragmented security institutions, and external rivalries." Mogadishu's position has hardened since. In an Al Jazeera interview on 3 October, President Mohamud said that Somalia would accept no Israeli presence in any circumstances and would resist attempts to draw it into Middle Eastern crises. Washington has been more cautious: after Israel's move, President Trump said he opposed US recognition of Somaliland. It would be simplistic to assume that every foreign government operates as part of a single anti-Somalia strategy. States have distinct interests and shifting alignments. Nevertheless, recognition disputes, port agreements, and security partnerships can reinforce one another, making Somalia's domestic divisions harder to resolve. Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Eritrea, and the UAE-Israel alignment Chatham House's analysis identifies a broad, fluid alignment of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey on one side, and the UAE and Israel on the other, with Eritrea and Ethiopia positioned within the wider picture. These are analytical descriptions, not fixed military blocs with identical objectives. Egypt's interest in Somalia reflects its concerns in the Horn and its dispute with Ethiopia over the Nile. Saudi Arabia's role is also significant: Mogadishu's termination of the UAE agreements came amid Saudi-Emirati tensions over Yemen, and Somalia subsequently pursued defense agreements with Qatar and Saudi Arabia . Disputes elsewhere thus reshape incentives in Somalia. The central risk is not alliances themselves but a regional security dilemma, in which one government's effort to strengthen an ally is read by another as a threat, prompting countermeasures that deepen the original insecurity. Somalia is especially vulnerable to this dynamic because its institutions are contested and its federal settlement is incomplete. Eritrea and Ethiopia occupy particularly sensitive positions because their regional relationships intersect with longstanding security concerns and competing interests in the Red Sea. Yet their positions cannot be reduced to a contest over Somalia; each government has its own domestic and regional priorities, and Somali leaders should avoid reading every foreign move as part of a single design. Danger of mediation gap The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) will cease operations on 31 October 2026, concluding a two-year transition requested by the federal government and approved by the Security Council. The UN announced the closure in its 27 October 2026 statement . At a ceremony in Mogadishu on 26 October, Deputy Prime Minister Saleh Ahmed Jama called the closure a historic day , saying Somalia had left the era of transition behind and now held most of its own security in its hands. The mission's functions have been handed over to Somali institutions, the UN country team, and the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS), ending thirteen years of engagement that began with UNSOM in 2013. UN agencies and UNSOS will continue their work, including support to the African Union mission. The Secretary-General has nonetheless warned that significant political, security, humanitarian, and development challenges remain. The transition coincides with an acute confrontation. The Associated Press reported on 29 October that the mission was closing without an agreed replacement positioned to mediate the election dispute, that UN-backed talks had failed, and that the president had invited leaders to further discussions in November. Somali institutions must now take greater responsibility for resolving disputes, yet they are themselves at the center of the disagreement. The African Union and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) therefore have important roles in supporting an inclusive settlement. The African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) is a separate security operation. Under UN Security Council Resolution 2809 (2025) , its authorization runs until 31 December 2026, with up to 11,826 uniformed personnel. Its logistics are under pressure: Reuters, as relayed by Berliner Zeitung , reported that Washington will no longer back UN logistical support to the mission from 1 January 2027. AUSSOM's counterterrorism role cannot substitute for political reconciliation. The priority is to ensure that the UN exit leaves no vacuum in political facilitation: IGAD, the African Union, the UN, and trusted partners should coordinate rather than compete and support a Somali-owned process that includes federal authorities and the opposition, including Puntland and Jubaland, whose absence from earlier talks limited their results. Al-Shabaab and ISIS-Somalia: Beneficiaries of political fragmentation The most immediate security cost of prolonged confrontation may be a weaker campaign against extremist groups. Al-Shabaab, an al-Qaeda affiliate, remains a major threat, and ISIS-Somalia is active, particularly in Puntland. When federal and regional authorities are preoccupied with each other, troops may be diverted, intelligence-sharing may weaken, and communities may lose confidence in institutions that seem more concerned with political survival than public protection. The Council on Foreign Relations' conflict tracker recorded on 19 October that the Speaker of Parliament accused politicians of colluding with Al-Shabaab, a sign of how deeply security and politics have become entangled. Somalia does not have to choose between international partnerships and national sovereignty." Chatham House warns that armed confrontation between the government and opposition could give extremist groups room to regroup. The risks are interconnected: political fragmentation weakens local administration, disrupts trade, increases displacement, and undermines cooperation between communities and security forces. They may exploit fragmentation even without substantial foreign support, and competition among external partners can redirect attention toward rival political clients and away from common security objectives. Partners should therefore avoid treating support for particular administrations as a substitute for a coordinated national security strategy. Civilians caught between political, geopolitical struggles Somali civilians have endured decades of conflict, displacement, drought, flooding, and economic insecurity. Renewed fighting in Mogadishu, Baidoa, or other contested areas would disrupt markets, schools, healthcare, and humanitarian access and expose civilians to shelling, airstrikes, and displacement; the June fighting in Mogadishu already sent residents fleeing. The closure of UNTMIS comes amid political uncertainty, extremist violence, climate emergencies, and shrinking humanitarian resources. A protracted conflict would also deter investment, disrupt trade, and divert public funds to military spending, leaving communities already affected by insecurity with fewer jobs and schools. External powers should therefore judge their engagement not only by strategic influence but also by its effects on civilian protection, economic resilience, and the capacity of Somali institutions to deliver services. The test of any foreign partnership should be whether it strengthens the security and welfare of Somalis rather than deepening the divisions that endanger them. Conclusion: Somalia as architect of its own regional relationships Somalia's crisis is not an inevitable march toward another civil war, and foreign competition is not the only explanation for its instability. The principal responsibility rests with Somali leaders, who must resolve their constitutional disputes, negotiate the distribution of authority, and prevent armed confrontation from replacing compromise. The country is grappling with contentious constitutional amendments that extend presidential terms and alter electoral processes, leading to disputes between the federal government and opposition groups. As the government asserts its authority, opposition leaders claim the president's mandate has expired, heightening tensions. The situation is complicated by external influences, with foreign nations backing different Somali factions, which risks transforming a domestic dispute into a broader conflict. The strategic significance of Somalia's coastline, vital for global trade routes, attracts international interest, further entangling local politics with foreign agendas. The ongoing instability threatens to undermine Somalia's sovereignty and complicate efforts for a unified national framework. As the UN political mission concludes, the potential for violence looms, with calls for negotiations remaining unfulfilled amid deepening divisions.

ethiopia.content: Contract Farming Modestly Improves Smallholder Food Security in Northwest HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 12, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Agriculture Contract Farming Modestly Improves Smallholder Food Security in Northwest Ethiopia by November 12, 2026 in Agriculture Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Contract Farming Modestly Improves Smallholder Food Security in Northwest Ethiopia Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram A scientific study examining smallholder agriculture in northwest Ethiopia has found that participation in contract farming for oilseed and pulse production yields small but statistically significant gains in household food and nutrition security. Published in Discover Food by researchers Marta Mohammed and Mengistie Mossie, the empirical investigation evaluated the direct welfare outcomes of formal institutional buyer agreements among rural agrarian households. Relative to non-participating producers, households engaged in oilseed and pulse contracts achieved higher dietary diversity and improved overall food consumption scores, demonstrating that structured commercial production arrangements can provide measurable nutritional benefits within smallholder farming communities. The research addresses a prominent knowledge gap in agricultural development strategies concerning high-value crop commercialization. While the cultivation of high-value crops is frequently promoted throughout Ethiopia as an essential pathway to advance agricultural development, the particular consequences of contractual arrangements for oilseed and pulse producers have remained under-researched. To address this deficiency, Mohammed and Mossie examined how formal oilseed and pulse contracts specifically impact household dietary diversity and food consumption status, testing whether commercial integration effectively supports household nutrition among smallholders in northwest Ethiopia. To evaluate these socioeconomic relationships, the authors gathered primary survey data from a sample of 329 randomly selected rural households across northwest Ethiopia. The empirical framework employed two principal analytical approaches to evaluate the collected information: descriptive analysis and average treatment effect estimation. By utilizing econometric average treatment effect modeling alongside descriptive methods, the researchers were able to assess the specific contributions of contract participation, comparing outcome metrics between contracting households and non-participating households while controlling for key household characteristics and socioeconomic variables. The descriptive analysis uncovered a pronounced divergence in perceptions and attitudes between participating smallholders and non-participants. Participating farmers held overwhelmingly favorable views of oilseed and pulse production contracts, with approximately 96 percent expressing positive attitudes toward their contractual agreements. These participants highlighted several major structural advantages associated with contract engagement, specifically identifying reliable access to essential farm inputs, production credit, agricultural extension services, and guaranteed output markets featuring price premiums. By contrast, only 20 percent of non-participating farmers viewed such production contracts favorably, with non-participants predominantly treating buyer-farmer agreements with indifference and deep-seated mistrust. The study’s econometric modeling provided detailed insights into the specific demographic and institutional determinants governing whether smallholders choose to participate in contract farming. The model results demonstrated that educational attainment, farm size, livestock ownership, direct contact with extension services, and institutional awareness significantly increase the likelihood that a household will enter an oilseed or pulse contract. Conversely, specific logistical and household constraints significantly reduced the probability of participation. In particular, greater physical distance to agricultural collecting centers and higher household dependency ratios were both found to significantly lower participation rates among smallholders. Regarding direct food and nutrition outcomes, the econometric estimations confirmed that contract participation provides statistically significant food security enhancements over non-participation, although the absolute scale of these improvements remains small. Engaging in oilseed and pulse contracts increased household food diversity scores by 0.36 and elevated household food consumption scores by 1.9 relative to non-participating households. These numerical metrics indicate that while contractual arrangements generate genuine, measurable progress in diversifying household diets and enhancing total food consumption, the nutritional shifts represent incremental advancements rather than dramatic transformations. In their concluding assessment, the researchers emphasized that contract farming should be viewed as an avenue for incremental progress rather than an immediate remedy for broader rural nutritional challenges. The evidence indicates that oilseed and pulse contracts offer the possibility of delivering marginal improvements to food and nutrition security for smallholder farmers, provided that complementary interventions are implemented. Specifically, the authors concluded that public policies must be enhanced and targeted awareness programs expanded to overcome non-participant skepticism, mitigate logistical barriers, and maximize the nutritional potential of contract farming initiatives across rural Ethiopia. Researchers Marta Mohammed and Mengistie Mossie found that these farmers experienced statistically significant gains in dietary diversity and overall food consumption compared to non-participants. The study, which surveyed 329 rural households, revealed that 96% of participating farmers viewed their contracts positively, citing benefits such as access to farm inputs and guaranteed markets. However, only 20% of non-participants shared this sentiment, often expressing skepticism. The study identified key factors influencing participation, including education, farm size, and access to extension services. While the improvements in food security were noted, they were described as incremental rather than transformative. The authors advocate for enhanced public policies and awareness programs to address barriers and maximize the potential benefits of contract farming for smallholders in the region.

somalia.content: Somalia repatriates 170 stranded migrants from Libya with EU support - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia repatriates 170 stranded migrants from Libya with EU support Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Wednesday November 11, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali federal government welcomed home 170 migrants repatriated from Libya on Tuesday through a European Union-supported voluntary return program, allowing them to reunite with their families after months stranded in the North African country. The operation was carried out in coordination with the federal government and supported by the European Union in Somalia through the Voluntary Humanitarian Return program, which assists vulnerable migrants seeking to return safely to their home countries. The returnees included children and young adults who had endured difficult conditions during irregular migration journeys and while stranded in Libya. advertisements Interior, Federal Affairs and Reconciliation Minister Ali Yusuf Ali Hoosh said the migrants had faced serious humanitarian challenges, including exploitation by human traffickers and harsh conditions in detention facilities. Some of the returnees were experiencing health problems following their experiences in Libya, according to officials involved in the operation. “The government and its partners had prepared assistance programs to help the returning migrants rebuild their lives in Somalia,” Hoosh said. The planned support includes medical care, employment opportunities and other reintegration services aimed at helping returnees recover and become economically self-sufficient. The European Union in Somalia described the return as safe, voluntary and dignified, emphasizing the importance of protecting migrants from trafficking and abuse while helping them reunite with their families. The EU-supported program aims to provide vulnerable migrants with an opportunity to return home and rebuild their lives after experiencing hardship abroad. Hoosh urged Somali youth to avoid dangerous irregular migration routes, warning that journeys across deserts and the Mediterranean Sea expose migrants to human trafficking, exploitation, detention and other life-threatening risks. He also encouraged the returnees not to lose hope and to take advantage of opportunities available in Somalia. The reception operation involved several Somali government agencies, including the Immigration and Citizenship Agency, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation and the Somali Police Force, alongside international partners supporting the return program. Libya has long served as a major transit point for migrants attempting to reach Europe through the Mediterranean Sea, including Somalis seeking better economic opportunities or fleeing insecurity. Migrants traveling through Libya frequently face risks including arbitrary detention, exploitation by trafficking networks and dangerous sea crossings. The latest return operation forms part of continuing efforts by the Somali government and international partners to assist vulnerable citizens stranded abroad and support their voluntary return and reintegration into their communities. somalia.content: Somalia seeks $6.3 billion in climate adaptation funding through 2035 - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia seeks $6.3 billion in climate adaptation funding through 2035 Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Thursday November 12, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has called for the early release of disaster preparedness funds and easier access to international climate financing, saying Somalia needs an estimated $6.3 billion to adapt to climate change through 2035. Addressing world leaders at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, on Wednesday, Hassan Sheikh urged wealthy countries to fulfill their climate commitments and provide greater support to nations facing severe droughts, floods and other climate-related disasters. advertisements “Somalia contributes only a small share of global greenhouse gas emissions but remains among the countries most vulnerable to the consequences of climate change,” the president said. He called on countries historically responsible for the largest share of emissions to take greater responsibility for financing efforts to reduce climate risks and protect vulnerable populations. Hassan Sheikh emphasized the importance of making disaster preparedness funds available as soon as weather forecasts indicate an approaching emergency, rather than waiting until communities have already suffered losses. He argued that early financing would enable vulnerable countries to prepare for disasters, protect livelihoods and reduce the humanitarian and economic damage caused by extreme weather. The president also called for climate financing to be provided primarily through grants rather than loans, warning that additional debt could place further pressure on countries already struggling with limited financial resources. “I urge international financial institutions and climate funds to simplify their application procedures and establish eligibility criteria that reflect countries' exposure to climate hazards,” he added. Hassan Sheikh estimated that Somalia would require approximately $6.3 billion through 2035 to finance climate adaptation measures, including efforts to strengthen resilience against droughts and floods. Somalia has experienced repeated climate-related emergencies in recent years, with prolonged droughts and severe flooding damaging farmland, killing livestock, displacing communities and worsening food insecurity. The country's dependence on rain-fed agriculture and livestock production makes rural households particularly vulnerable to changing rainfall patterns and extreme weather. For Somalia, access to predictable climate financing is considered essential to expanding early warning systems, improving water management, protecting agricultural livelihoods and strengthening disaster preparedness. Hassan Sheikh's remarks came during the high-level segment of COP31, which brings together heads of state and government to discuss international climate commitments and support for countries most affected by global warming. The conference began Nov. 9 and runs through Nov. 20, with negotiations focusing on climate finance, adaptation, emissions reductions and implementation of the Paris Agreement. Ghana's national football team has welcomed back key players Mohammed Kudus, Jordan Ayew, Thomas Partey, and Mohammed Salisu for their crucial 2026 World Cup qualifier against Somalia. The match, scheduled for October 12, is vital for Ghana's hopes of advancing in the qualification process. Coach Chris Hughton expressed confidence in the squad's strength with the return of these experienced players, who have been instrumental in previous matches. Kudus, currently playing for West Ham United, has been in impressive form, while Ayew and Partey bring valuable leadership and experience. Salisu's inclusion adds depth to the defense. The team aims to secure a decisive victory to boost their standing in the group. Fans are optimistic about the players' return, hoping it will enhance Ghana's chances of qualifying for the World Cup. The match will take place at the Accra Sports Stadium, where a strong home crowd is expected to support the Black Stars. 

(151 words)

somalia.summary: Burundi is expediting the withdrawal of its troops from Somalia, where they have been part of the African Union peacekeeping mission since 2007. The Burundian contingent has relied heavily on logistical support from the United Nations, which is crucial as they prepare to leave. The urgency of this withdrawal comes as the African Union's Somalia mission (AUSSOM) is set to conclude. Despite the challenges, including a lack of a fallback plan for continued operations, the Burundian government is moving forward with its exit strategy. This development highlights the ongoing complexities in Somalia's security landscape, as the country grapples with political instability and the presence of militant groups. The situation remains fluid, with international stakeholders closely monitoring the implications of Burundi's troop withdrawal on the overall stability of the region.

somalia.content: AUSSOM chief, Swedish ambassador discuss Somalia security and international support - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY AUSSOM chief, Swedish ambassador discuss Somalia security and international support Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Wednesday November 11, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — The head of the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) met Sweden’s ambassador to Somalia on Monday to discuss the country’s security situation, implementation of the mission’s mandate and continued international support for peace and stabilization efforts. Amb. El Hadji Ibrahima Diene, the special representative of the African Union Commission chairperson SRCC and Head of AUSSOM, met Swedish Ambassador Hans Lundquist in Mogadishu, according to the mission. The two officials reviewed recent developments in Somalia and discussed cooperation between AUSSOM, the Federal Government and international partners. advertisements Diene praised Sweden’s longstanding engagement with Somalia and the African Union, including support for peacebuilding and stabilization. Lundquist reaffirmed Sweden’s commitment to working with the Somali government, AUSSOM and international partners to advance sustainable peace and stability. Sweden has maintained development and humanitarian engagement with Somalia for decades. Its current cooperation strategy for 2026-2028 includes support for state-building, democratic governance, human rights, resilience and economic opportunities. AUSSOM, which replaced the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia in January 2025, is mandated to support Somali security forces, help degrade al-Shabab, protect key population centers and infrastructure, and assist Somalia’s broader security transition. Diene currently heads the mission as the African Union Commission chairperson’s special representative for Somalia. The meeting comes as AUSSOM continues to rely heavily on international financial and political support while Somalia gradually assumes greater responsibility for national security. somalia.title: Somalia, Türkiye discuss security cooperation and counterterrorism efforts - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somalia, Türkiye discuss security cooperation and counterterrorism efforts - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY Somalia, Türkiye discuss security cooperation and counterterrorism efforts Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Wednesday November 11, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia and Türkiye discussed military and security developments, counterterrorism operations and bilateral security cooperation during talks in Mogadishu, as the two countries seek to deepen a longstanding defense partnership. Türkiye’s ambassador to Somalia, Ferhat Alkan, met National Security Adviser Awes Hagi Yusuf Ahmed on Tuesday for talks focused on Somalia’s security situation and efforts against al-Shabab, according to statements from the Turkish Embassy and Somali officials. The meeting also covered political developments and broader security coordination between Ankara and Mogadishu. advertisements “Türkiye remains committed to contributing to Somalia’s peace, stability and security, as it has done in the past and continues to do today,” the Turkish Embassy said. Somalia’s National Security Adviser expressed appreciation for Türkiye’s longstanding support and stressed the importance of continued coordination between the two governments, according to Anadolu Agency. The talks come as Somalia continues military operations against al-Shabab while also navigating changes in the international security presence supporting the country. Türkiye is one of Somalia’s closest security partners and operates the TURKSOM military training facility in Mogadishu, which has trained thousands of Somali soldiers and officers. Turkish support has included military training, logistical assistance and institution-building for Somalia’s armed forces. Alkan also met Somali Defense Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi this week, with discussions focused on strengthening defense cooperation, building the capacity of the Somali National Armed Forces and reviewing regional security developments. The Somali government has described Türkiye as a strategic partner in its efforts to strengthen national security institutions and reduce reliance on foreign forces. Alkan assumed his post as Türkiye’s ambassador to Somalia on Sept. 21, succeeding Alper Aktaş. Türkiye’s ambassador to Somalia, Ferhat Alkan, met with Somalia’s National Security Adviser, Awes Hagi Yusuf Ahmed, to address the current security landscape and the importance of ongoing collaboration between the two nations. The Turkish Embassy reaffirmed Türkiye's commitment to supporting Somalia's peace and stability, highlighting its historical role in military training and logistical assistance. The talks also included discussions with Somali Defense Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi on strengthening defense ties and building the capacity of the Somali National Armed Forces. Türkiye operates the TURKSOM military training facility in Mogadishu, which has trained thousands of Somali personnel. The Somali government views Türkiye as a strategic partner in bolstering national security and reducing dependence on foreign military forces. These discussions come amid Somalia's ongoing military operations against al-Shabab and shifts in international security support. (157 words)

football.summary: أعلنت لجنة الاستئناف بالاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم قرارًا مفاجئًا بشأن لقب الدوري السوداني، حيث ألغت قرارها السابق الذي منح اللقب لنادي المريخ، وأعادت اللقب لنادي الهلال. جاء هذا القرار بعد قبول طلب المراجعة المقدم من الهلال، الذي أكد استحقاقه للقب بعد فوزه على المريخ في المباراة الأخيرة من الموسم الماضي. وأوضحت اللجنة أنها عقدت اجتماعين في 9 و10 نوفمبر، حيث استندت إلى تقرير الحكم في المباراة. وأصدر نادي الهلال بيانًا رسميًا يعلن فيه استرداده للقب، مؤكدًا مكانته كأكثر الأندية تتويجًا بالبطولات في السودان. يذكر أن الموسم الماضي شهد جدلًا كبيرًا حول قانونية مشاركة بعض لاعبي الهلال، مما أدى إلى منح اللقب للمريخ بعد استئناف. هذا القرار يعيد الأمور إلى نصابها ويؤكد تفوق الهلال في الساحة الرياضية السودانية.

football.title: باللجوء للمحكمة الرياضية.. أزمة سحب لقب الدوري السوداني من المريخ تتصاعد - متن نيوز
football.content: زمة سحب لقب الدوري السوداني من المريخ تتصاعد الخميس 12 نوفمبر 2026 facebook twitter youtube instagram whatsapp rss feed احدث الاخبار تلفزيون متن الرياضة السياسة الاقتصاد تقارير وتحقيقات الدراسات والابحاث باللجوء للمحكمة الرياضية.. أزمة سحب لقب الدوري السوداني من المريخ تتصاعد المريخ السوداني الأربعاء 11/نوفمبر/2026 - 06:03 م 11/11/2026 6:03:24 PM الرياضة شارك طباعة أكد نادي المريخ السوداني، على رفضه القاطع لقرار لجنة الاستئناف المتعلق بشأن لقب الدوري للموسم الماضي، بعد قبول اللجنة لطلب الفحص من الهلال. وأعلن نادي الهلال مساء أمس الثلاثاء، حصوله على لقب الدوري السوداني الموسم الماضي، بقرار رسمي صادر من قبل لجنة الاستئناف في الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم. وشدد المريخ السوداني في بيانه الرسمي الذي أصدره عبر صفحاته الرسمية، على رفضه القاطع لقرار لجنة الاستئنافات، مؤكدًا على تصعيد القضية إلى محكمة التحكيم الرياضية "كاس". وجاء بيان المريخ السوداني كالتالي: "يعلن نادي المريخ الرياضي رفضه القاطع لقرار لجنة الاستئنافات المشكلة حديثًا، والقاضي بقبول طلب الفحص المقدم من النادي الآخر، ونقض القرار السابق الذي قضى بأحقية المريخ في لقب بطولة الدوري الممتاز، وبذلك يؤكد تمسكه بكافة حقوقه ومكتسباته، ورفضه لأي إجراءات تنتقص منها". وواصل في بيانه الرسمي: "ويثير القرار استغراب المجلس، لا سيما أن لجنة الاستئنافات السابقة لم تكتفِ بإصدار قرارها لصالح المريخ، بل أشادت في حيثياته بالاستئناف الذي تقدم به النادي، وأثبتت ذلك صراحة في مضابطها، وهو الأمر الذي قاد الاتحاد السوداني إلى إجراء تعديلات على لائحة أوضاع اللاعبين استنادًا إلى ما انتهت إليه اللجنة للقضية، الأمر الذي يجعل العدول عن ذلك القرار موضع تساؤل قانوني". وأردف في البيان الرسمي: "وتزداد علامات الاستفهام حول القرار الأخير، في ظل تلقي النادي إخطارًا رسميًا من الاتحاد يفيد بانتقال القضية إلى محكمة التحكيم الرياضية الدولية (CAS)، بناءً على الشكوى المقدمة من النادي الآخر بالرقم A/12688. وهو ما يطرح تساؤلات جوهرية حول الأساس القانوني والإجرائي لإعادة النظر في القضية أمام لجنة الاستئنافات، بعد إخطار الأطراف بانتقال النزاع إلى المحكمة الدولية". واستكمل المريخ في بيانه: "وبناءً على كل ذلك وعلى ضوء القرار الأخير حسم مجلس إدارة نادي المريخ أمره وقرر تصعيد القضية إلى محكمة التحكيم الرياضية الدولية (CAS)، والمضي في كافة الإجراءات القانونية اللازمة، مستندًا إلى خبرات النادي وتجاربه السابقة أمام المحكمة، ومستعينًا بالكفاءات القانونية المتخصصة، دفاعًا عن حقه في البطولة حتى صدور القرار النهائي". وأردف النادي السوداني في بيانه: "وفي هذا الصدد يوجه المجلس وجماهير النادي ورموزه ونجومه وإعلامه وكافة قطاعاته رسالة واضحة إلى الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم، بأن المريخ نادٍ جماهيري وقيادي، له تاريخه ومكانته وقاعدته الممتدة داخل السودان وخارجه، لذلك لن يقبل المساس بحقوقه أو الانتقاص من مقدراته". واستكمل: "وعلى الاتحاد الالتزام بمسؤولياته في إدارة المنافسة بعدالة وأخلاق وحياد، إضافة إلى تطبيق اللوائح دون تمييز أو انتقائية، ونعيد التأكيد بأقوى العبارات أن المريخ لن يقف مكتوف الأيدي أمام أي إجراءات تمس حقوقه، ولن يقبل فرض الأمر الواقع عليه أو العبث بمكتسباته، وسيواجه ذلك بكل الوسائل القانونية والمؤسسية المتاحة". واختتم النادي بيانه: "وإلى جماهير المريخ الوفية، يؤكد المجلس أن حقوق النادي ليست محل مساومة أو تفريط، وأنه ماضٍ في طريق القانون حتى النهاية، وأنتم من خلفنا سندًا والعهد بيننا ألا تراجع إطلاقًا". وقد حسم الدوري السوداني في الموسم الماضي، بشكل مثير للجدل، حيث توج المريخ باللقب رغم فوز الهلال بهدف نظيف في الجولة الأخيرة من البطولة، وجاء ذلك بعد قبول استئناف المريخ ضد قرار لجنة المسابقات بشأن قانونية مشاركة عدد من لاعبي الهلال خلال مباراة القمة بين الفريقين. شارك المريخ السوداني الهلال لجنة الاستئناف نادي المريخ الدوري السوداني الأكثر مشاهدة محمد فريد يكشف تفاصيل استراتيجية جديدة للترويج للاستثمار تستهدف 16 قطاعًا اقتصاديًا استراتيجية استثمارية تستهدف 16 قطاعًا.. تفاصيل تحركات مصر لجذب football.summary: تتصاعد أزمة سحب لقب الدوري السوداني من نادي المريخ بعد قرار لجنة الاستئناف بقبول طلب نادي الهلال للفحص، مما أدى إلى إعلان الهلال فوزه باللقب. نادي المريخ، في بيان رسمي، أعرب عن رفضه القاطع لهذا القرار وأكد عزمه تصعيد القضية إلى محكمة التحكيم الرياضية الدولية (CAS). وأشار المريخ إلى أن القرار الأخير يثير تساؤلات قانونية، خاصة بعد أن أشادت اللجنة السابقة بقرارها لصالحه. كما أكد النادي أنه لن يقبل أي إجراءات تمس حقوقه، مشددًا على أهمية إدارة المنافسة بعدالة وحياد. المريخ يعتزم اتخاذ كافة الإجراءات القانونية اللازمة للدفاع عن حقه في البطولة، مع التأكيد على دعم جماهيره. الدوري السوداني شهد جدلًا كبيرًا حول لقبه، حيث توج المريخ رغم فوز الهلال في الجولة الأخيرة، بعد قبول استئناف المريخ بشأن قانونية مشاركة بعض لاعبي الهلال.

football.title: المريخ السوداني يعلن التصعيد إلى المحكمة الرياضية بعد سحب لقب الدوري - Masrawy
football.content: المريخ السوداني يصعّد أزمة لقب الدوري إلى المحكمة الرياضية الرئيسية رياضة رياضة عالمية المريخ السوداني يعلن التصعيد إلى المحكمة الرياضية بعد سحب لقب الدوري 12:48 م الأربعاء 11 نوفمبر 2026 فريق المريخ السوداني أعلن نادي المريخ السوداني رفضه القاطع لقرار لجنة الاستئنافات بالاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم، بشأن سحب لقب الدوري الممتاز للموسم الماضي ومنحه لمنافسه الهلال، مؤكدًا عزمه تصعيد القضية إلى محكمة التحكيم الرياضية الدولية «كاس» (CAS). إعلان وكانت لجنة الاستئنافات قد أصدرت قرارًا بقبول طلب الفحص المقدم من نادي الهلال، ونقض القرار السابق الذي منح المريخ أحقية التتويج بلقب الدوري، ليعلن الهلال مساء أمس الثلاثاء حصوله رسميًا على البطولة. وتعود تفاصيل الأزمة إلى الجولة الأخيرة من منافسات الدوري السوداني الموسم الماضي، عندما حقق الهلال الفوز على المريخ بهدف دون مقابل، إلا أن الأخير تُوّج باللقب بعد قبول استئنافه ضد قرار لجنة المسابقات بشأن قانونية مشاركة عدد من لاعبي الهلال في مباراة القمة بين الفريقين. المريخ يتمسك بالتصعيد إلى المحكمة الرياضية وأكد مجلس إدارة المريخ، في بيان رسمي نشره عبر منصاته، رفضه قرار لجنة الاستئنافات، مشددًا على تمسكه بكافة حقوقه ومكتسباته، واعتباره القرار الأخير محل تساؤلات قانونية وإجرائية. وأشار النادي إلى أن لجنة الاستئنافات السابقة سبق أن أصدرت قرارًا لصالحه، بل أشادت في حيثياتها بالاستئناف الذي تقدم به، وهو ما دفع الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم إلى إجراء تعديلات على لائحة أوضاع اللاعبين استنادًا إلى ما انتهت إليه اللجنة في القضية. وأضاف البيان أن علامات الاستفهام تتزايد بشأن القرار الجديد، خاصة بعدما تلقى النادي إخطارًا رسميًا من الاتحاد السوداني يفيد بانتقال النزاع إلى محكمة التحكيم الرياضية الدولية، بناءً على الشكوى المقدمة من الهلال، والمسجلة تحت الرقم A/12688. وأوضح المريخ أن هذا الإجراء يثير تساؤلات بشأن الأساس القانوني لإعادة فتح القضية أمام لجنة الاستئنافات، بعد إخطار الأطراف بانتقال النزاع إلى المحكمة الرياضية الدولية. المريخ: لن نفرط في حقوق النادي وشدد مجلس إدارة النادي على اتخاذ قرار نهائي بتصعيد القضية إلى محكمة التحكيم الرياضية الدولية، والمضي في جميع الإجراءات القانونية اللازمة، بالاستعانة بخبرات قانونية متخصصة، للدفاع عن أحقية الفريق في اللقب حتى صدور الحكم النهائي. كما وجّه المجلس رسالة إلى الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم، مطالبًا إياه بالالتزام بمسؤولياته في إدارة المسابقات وفق مبادئ العدالة والحياد، وتطبيق اللوائح دون تمييز أو انتقائية. واختتم المريخ بيانه بالتأكيد على أن حقوق النادي ليست محل مساومة أو تفريط، وأنه سيواصل اتخاذ المسارات القانونية والمؤسسية المتاحة للدفاع عن موقفه، مع توجيه رسالة طمأنة إلى جماهيره بأن المجلس متمسك بالقضية حتى النهاية. المريخ السوداني الهلال الدوري السوداني إعلان الأخبار المتعلقة شباب أهلي دبي يعلن جاهزيته لمواجهة الهلال السعودي في دوري أبطال النخبة يصعّد أزمة لقب الدوري إلى المحكمة الرياضية الدولية «كاس» المريخ السوداني يصعّد أزمة لقب الدوري إلى المحكمة الرياضية الدولية «كاس» ميدو حسين 70 مشاهدة أعلن نادي المريخ السوداني رفضه التام لقرار لجنة الاستئنافات بالاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم، بشأن حسم لقب الدوري الممتاز للموسم الماضي، وذلك عقب قبول طلب الفحص المقدم من نادي الهلال، وإلغاء القرار السابق الذي منح المريخ أحقية التتويج بالبطولة. وكان نادي الهلال السوداني قد أعلن مساء أمس الثلاثاء حصوله رسميًا على لقب الدوري الممتاز للموسم الماضي، بعد صدور قرار من لجنة الاستئنافات بالاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم، يقضي بقبول طلب الفحص المقدم من النادي. وفي المقابل، أصدر مجلس إدارة المريخ بيانًا رسميًا عبر منصاته المختلفة، أكد خلاله رفضه القاطع للقرار الأخير، مشددًا على تمسكه بحقه في لقب البطولة، واتخاذه قرارًا باللجوء إلى محكمة التحكيم الرياضية الدولية «CAS» لمواصلة المعركة القانونية. وأوضح النادي في بيانه أن قرار لجنة الاستئنافات الجديدة تضمن قبول طلب الفحص المقدم من الهلال، وإلغاء الحكم السابق الذي أقر بأحقية المريخ في التتويج بلقب الدوري الممتاز، مؤكدًا أن مجلس الإدارة لن يتنازل عن حقوق النادي أو أي من مكتسباته. وأشار المريخ إلى أن موقفه يستند إلى ما صدر عن لجنة الاستئنافات السابقة، التي أصدرت قرارًا لصالحه، وأشادت في حيثيات حكمها بالاستئناف الذي تقدم به النادي، وهو ما تم إثباته في محاضرها الرسمية، لافتًا إلى أن الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم أجرى تعديلات على لائحة أوضاع اللاعبين استنادًا إلى ما انتهت إليه اللجنة في القضية، الأمر الذي يضع قرار التراجع عن الحكم السابق أمام العديد من التساؤلات القانونية. وأضاف البيان أن علامات الاستفهام تتزايد بشأن القرار الأخير، خاصة أن النادي سبق أن تلقى إخطارًا رسميًا من الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم يفيد بإحالة النزاع إلى محكمة التحكيم الرياضية الدولية، بناءً على الشكوى المقدمة من الهلال تحت رقم A/12688، وهو ما يثير تساؤلات حول المبررات القانونية والإجرائية التي استندت إليها لجنة الاستئنافات في إعادة فتح الملف، رغم إخطار الأطراف بانتقال القضية إلى المحكمة الدولية. وأكد مجلس إدارة المريخ أنه حسم موقفه باللجوء إلى المحكمة الرياضية الدولية «كاس»، مع اتخاذ جميع الإجراءات القانونية اللازمة، والاستعانة بمجموعة من المتخصصين في القضايا الرياضية، مستندًا إلى خبرات النادي السابقة في التعامل مع المحكمة، بهدف الحفاظ على حقوقه والمطالبة باللقب حتى صدور الحكم النهائي. ووجّه مجلس الإدارة رسالة إلى الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم، أكد خلالها أن المريخ يمتلك تاريخًا كبيرًا ومكانة جماهيرية ورياضية داخل السودان وخارجه، ولن يسمح بالمساس بحقوقه أو الانتقاص من مكتسباته، مشددًا على ضرورة تحمل الاتحاد مسؤولياته في إدارة المسابقات وفقًا لمبادئ العدالة والنزاهة والحياد. كما طالب النادي الاتحاد السوداني بتطبيق اللوائح والقوانين على جميع الأندية دون تمييز أو انتقائية، مؤكدًا أنه لن يقبل فرض أي قرارات كأمر واقع، وأنه سيستخدم كافة الوسائل القانونية والمؤسسية المتاحة للدفاع عن حقوقه. واختتم المريخ بيانه بتوجيه رسالة إلى جماهيره، شدد خلالها على أن حقوق النادي ليست قابلة للتفاوض أو التنازل، وأن مجلس الإدارة مستمر في اتخاذ المسارات القانونية حتى النهاية، معربًا عن ثقته في مساندة جماهيره خلال المرحلة المقبلة، ومؤكدًا تمسكه بالقضية حتى حسمها بصورة نهائية. المريخ السوداني الهلال السوداني الاتحاد
